posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: CRO at a financial firm banning ChatGPT over explainability — validate the compliance pain and add the 'auditability is the actual product' insight, with three ICP prospects watching
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is the moment the whole thing unravels. It's not really a trust problem — it's an audit trail problem. Black-box outputs were always going to hit a wall in regulated industries, and I think a lot of teams are only just figuring that out now. The question isn't whether to use AI in analytics, it's whether you can reconstruct every number when someone puts it under a microscope.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consulting firm describing the exact adoption problem Milo exists to solve — validate the pain with specificity, add the trust framing insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The dashboard was never the problem. It's that finance teams have been burned by numbers that looked right but weren't, and Excel at least feels like *their* numbers — they built it, they trust it. Eighteen months of build doesn't undo that. The question worth asking is: what would it actually take for your CFO to quote a dashboard number without double-checking it in a spreadsheet first?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard overload — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody looks' layer without pitching
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically saying 'we don't know what matters yet' but in spreadsheet form. The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells me it wasn't a behaviour problem — people just couldn't find a reason to come back. The dashboard that answers one question people actually ask every morning will always beat the one built to impress during the QBR. Curious what the 5 metrics ended up being?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: High-scoring post with an Innovation Director from a retail ICP engaging — validate the 'who owns the truth' framing with a sharper diagnosis, then leave a question that makes Lisa Kaur feel seen
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem is real but I think the root issue is even simpler — most teams skipped the hard conversation about definitions before they handed out the licences. Self-service works fine when everyone's pulling from the same agreed truth. The tool isn't the failure, the governance conversation that never happened is. Who actually owned that call in your org before the rollout?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org reframing hallucinations as security risk, with a CEO prospect engaged — validate the framing with a specific operational angle, add the trust-chain insight
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I don't think enough people in analytics are sitting with it yet. A hallucinated number doesn't announce itself — it looks identical to a real one, which means the risk isn't just in the output, it's in every downstream decision that never gets traced back to the source. User inputs get sanitised, validated, logged. Most AI-generated analytics outputs get... trusted. Who in your org actually owns the audit trail when a hallucinated figure makes it into a board deck?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: COO at a consulting firm is watching this thread — validate the £200k ghost platform pain with a specific observation about who BI tools are actually designed for, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number stings, but honestly the real cost is the six months before anyone admits it's not working. Most BI tools are designed to impress in a demo, not to survive contact with a finance manager who just wants to answer one question without filing a support ticket. The 'self-service' label has done a lot of damage — it sets an expectation that the tool will meet people where they are, when usually it's the opposite. How many of your clients have a BI tool that genuinely gets used by people who didn't build it?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial company nailing a real data governance pain point — validate the culture diagnosis, add the layer he's missing about why the filters diverged in the first place
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, three filter sets — that's not a culture problem yet, that's a definition problem. Nobody agreed on what 'this quarter' actually means before the dashboard got built. Culture is the fix, sure, but you need one moment where someone writes down the answer and everyone else stops arguing. The hard question is: who owns that moment in your org?

posts.post_text: Enterprise analytics teams are wasting 40% of their time on ad-hoc reporting requests. Our new AI-Powered Analytics eliminates the bottleneck entirely. See how Fortune 500 companies are scaling their data teams with ThoughtSpot. #analytics #enterprise
posts.angle: ThoughtSpot pushing AI as the bottleneck solution — challenge the assumption that the bottleneck is speed, not trust in the answers
posts.draft_comment: 40% sounds right, but I'd push back on the cause. Most ad-hoc requests I've seen aren't bottlenecked by how fast someone can pull data — they're bottlenecked by whether anyone trusts the number that comes back. Faster AI on top of a shaky foundation just means you get to the wrong answer quicker. Curious how David and Priya are thinking about that trust layer in practice?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' problem — validate the adoption failure pattern and add the insight that the prompt burden is the real design flaw, not user laziness
posts.draft_comment: 12% after 90 days is pretty much the industry average nobody talks about. The 'nobody knows what to ask' thing isn't a training problem — it's a product design problem. If you need to be an expert to use an expert tool, you've just built a faster way for experts to do what they already could. Curious what your 12% actually have in common — my guess is they already knew what they wanted before they opened it.
